title: Perfect joy (Little Flowers 8)
hook: Francis says perfect joy is being turned away in the cold and staying patient

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lady Poverty: Francis courting poverty the way a knight courts a lady. Your line was poor for love. What did you go without, and what did you notice when it was gone? Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

Winter, on a road in Umbria. Two friars are walking home to their little church, Saint Mary of the Angels: Francis, and Brother Leo a little way ahead. It is bitterly cold. Every so often Francis calls out. Brother Leo, write this down: if the friars everywhere gave a great example of holiness, that is not perfect joy. Further on: if a friar could heal the sick and make the blind see, write that this is not perfect joy. If he knew every language and every science, not perfect joy. If he preached so well that whole peoples came to faith, still not perfect joy. On and on, until Leo can't bear it and asks: then, Father, for God's sake, where is perfect joy? Today's word is the answer.
screen: `A ROAD IN WINTER.` → `NOT MIRACLES. NOT LEARNING.` → `THEN WHERE IS PERFECT JOY?`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Little Flowers of Saint Francis, a book of stories about Francis and his first companions. Here is his answer, told in his own roundabout way. When we reach Saint Mary of the Angels, soaked with rain, stiff with cold, muddy and hungry, we knock at the gate. The porter comes out angry and asks who we are. We say, two of your brothers. And he says, you're lying, you're a pair of tramps who go around stealing alms from the poor. He won't open. He leaves us out in the snow and the rain until night. If we bear that patiently, without grumbling, and think humbly that perhaps the porter knows us better than we know ourselves, Brother Leo, write that this is perfect joy. Francis even pushes it further: if the porter comes back with a knotted stick, and we bear that too, thinking of what Christ suffered, there is perfect joy. Then he explains. Everything on his list, the miracles, the learning, the preaching, is a gift from God. So there's nothing in it to boast about. He quotes Saint Paul to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "what hast thou that thou hast not received?" The one thing we can offer of our own, Francis says, is to bear a hardship for love of Christ. And he closes with Paul again: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." It helps to notice what Francis is not saying. He doesn't say the porter is right, or that cruelty is good. He's pulling joy apart from success, and from being recognized. The joy he means is the kind a locked gate can't take away.
screen: `SOAKED, FROZEN, TURNED AWAY.` · `BEAR IT PATIENTLY: PERFECT JOY.` · `EVERY GIFT WAS RECEIVED.` · `A JOY A LOCKED GATE CAN'T TAKE.` · then, large: `WHAT HAST THOU THAT THOU HAST NOT RECEIVED?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay patient when refused. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a recent no. A message left unanswered, a request turned down, a door that didn't open. Stand outside that door again for a moment, in your mind. Notice whatever rises, if anything does: heat, an argument, an it's not fair. You don't have to push it away. Just breathe beside it, the way Francis pictures standing in the snow. Then let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can offer that closed door to God. If you don't, simply rest in the breath outside the gate, without needing it to open. The bell holds the time.
Perfect joy. For Francis, not success or praise, but patience outside a closed gate, for love of Christ. Today's word.
Your line: perfect joy. Today, when something is refused you, even something small, take one slow breath before you answer, and see what's still there. Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Franciscan friars, sisters and lay Franciscans read the story of perfect joy from the Little Flowers, and some return to it when they meet rejection or hardship.

match.prompt: the road to the gate — tap the pairs.

myth: Francis says perfect joy is working miracles
he lists miracles, learning and great preaching, and says none of them is perfect joy.
Francis says the porter was right to shut them out
he never says the porter is right. he says patience outside the closed gate is perfect joy.
Francis quotes Saint Paul to explain himself
"what hast thou that thou hast not received?" every gift is God's; bearing hardship for Christ is what we can offer.

fork.setup: you're Brother Leo. for miles, in the cold, Francis has told you what perfect joy is not. what do you do?
options: ask him, for God's sake, where perfect joy is.
tell him you're too cold to listen.
fork.reveal: Leo finally asks, and Francis answers with a locked gate, an angry porter and a night in the snow, borne patiently.

original.note: Italian, the language of the Little Flowers: perfect joy, perfect gladness.

trapdoor: what you thought: perfect joy means everything going right.
what it means: for Francis, patience outside a locked gate, cold and refused, for love of Christ.
what a scholar hears: Francis sets every gift aside because each was received, with 1 Corinthians 4:7, and keeps only the cross, with Galatians 6:14.

sources.work: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis (Fioretti)

notes: The Fioretti chapter is paraphrased throughout. Check: the walk from Perugia to Saint Mary of the Angels in winter; Leo walking ahead; the list (example of holiness, healing and sight to the blind, all languages and sciences, preaching that converts unbelievers) each 'not perfect joy'; Leo asking where perfect joy is; the porter calling them vagabonds who steal alms from the poor; the snow and rain until night; the knotted stick; the conclusion quoting 1 Cor 4:7 and Gal 6:14.
Chapter numbering of the Fioretti varies between editions; the index title says ch. 8.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: 1 Corinthians 4:7 and Galatians 6:14.
The Italian 'perfetta letizia' is given as the original phrase; confirm.
The list in the hook is condensed (e.g. raising the dead and casting out devils are omitted).

Editor pass: the practice no longer tells the listener what rises in them ('notice whatever rises, if anything does'); text otherwise checked against the Fioretti summary and Douay-Rheims and left as written.
